column4: God knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it; this gives the section's burial-and-extraction movement as a single polarity under divine knowledge.
God knows what enters the earth and what emerges from it, directly matching the movement from a body placed below ground to grave contents brought out.
The deniers ask whether, after becoming lost within the earth, they can enter a new creation; this identifies the resurrection problem as bodily matter dispersed into its earthen container.

Believers are told to spend from good things and from what God has brought out of the earth, while refusing the bad; the ayah combines terrestrial extraction with discrimination between valuable and inferior material.
On the resurrection day even a mustard seed's weight is brought forth and accounted for; this supplies the exact moral weighing that follows the section's assay-like separation of hidden contents.
On the day people are presented, no hidden thing belonging to them remains hidden; it states the complete exposure toward which the opened graves and processed breasts move.

Hoarded gold and silver are heated in fire and used to brand their owners; the metal treated as precious in the section's mining image becomes an instrument that exposes and punishes misplaced valuation.

The ayah compares despair of the hereafter with despair concerning the occupants of graves; it presents the closed grave as an apparent boundary of hope that the section's opening of graves overturns.
Those plotting evil are warned that God may make the earth swallow them, the opposite vertical movement to earth casting out the concealed dead.
People on land are warned that God can cause the ground to swallow them; the secure surface becomes an entrance downward rather than the exit upward pictured by opened graves.
Among the punished peoples are those whom God caused the earth to swallow, a concise reversal of the section's earth releasing what it contains.
Deniers are warned that God could make the earth swallow them, setting downward concealment against the resurrection scene of bodies forced back out.
The threat that earth may swallow people while it heaves joins ingestion and violent ground movement, reversing the section's heaving earth that surrenders its contents.
Deeds thought to have value are made into scattered dust; this reverses the section's assay image, in which processing separates lasting value from surrounding earth.
The deeds of disbelievers are like ash driven violently by wind, a worthless airborne residue contrasting with useful matter that survives the section's separation process.
Pearls and coral emerge from the two waters, another Qur'anic scene in which valuable material comes forth from an encompassing medium.
After the earth is split in 80:26, grain is made to grow in it; this ayah identifies the useful content released by the opened agricultural soil.
God's purpose is to purify the believers and efface the disbelievers; the purification verb gives a moral counterpart to refining mixed material until its true value is isolated.
Hatred has appeared from hostile mouths while what their breasts conceal is greater, explicitly contrasting a visible sample with a larger inner deposit.
On judgment day the earth is pounded repeatedly, a forceful breaking and reworking of the ground that enlarges the section's hoof-struck surface into an eschatological event.
Earth and mountains are lifted and crushed in one crushing, presenting final ground upheaval as a total mechanical overturning of solid terrain.
Earth and mountains quake and the mountains become a loose mound of sand, a judgment-day counterpart to solid ground broken into mobile particles.
Humanity is produced from earth and settled or enabled to cultivate it, complementing the section's land-working sense of ث و ر and its contrast between worldly development and return to soil.
Rain revives earth after its death while winds and controlled clouds move above it; the ayah brings together stirred atmosphere and hidden terrestrial life emerging from inert ground.
Water sent from heaven gives life to earth after its death, a repeated concrete pattern for apparently inert soil releasing life.
Water revives earth after its death, preserving the section's hidden-to-living movement even though this ayah does not itself state the human resurrection comparison.
Rain gives life to earth after its death, another occurrence in the same surah that uses changing soil as evidence beside the ث و ر cloud and plowing scenes.
Provision sent from heaven revives earth after its death, making lifeless ground a receptacle whose latent outcome is brought forth.
God's reviving of earth after its death is offered as a sign to understand, supporting the section's passage from disturbed soil to the recovery of the dead.
Water is driven to barren land and crops are brought out for people and livestock, a direct agricultural instance of useful content extracted from earth.
Gold and silver are hoarded rather than spent before being heated in 9:35; this identifies the supposedly precious extracted material whose moral value is reversed by its use.
In an oath about the coming Hour, not even an atom's weight in earth escapes the Lord and all is recorded; hidden terrestrial minuteness cannot evade later accounting.
No atom's weight in earth escapes the Lord and nothing smaller or larger lies outside the record, joining concealed matter to exhaustive knowledge.
Nothing absent or hidden in heaven or earth falls outside the clear record, supporting the section's claim that buried contents remain fully recoverable.
Nothing in earth or heaven is hidden from God, stating the epistemic boundary that makes both grave contents and breast contents accessible.
On the resurrection day people are fully exposed and nothing concerning them is hidden from God, the human result of the section's physical and inward uncovering.
The scrolls are spread open in the same judgment sequence as the buried girl is questioned, giving documentary form to hidden contents being unfolded for inspection.
A staff strikes stone and twelve springs burst from it; striking a hard surface releases concealed matter, an indirect counterpart to hooves striking earth and sparks or soil springing forth.
When the stone is struck, twelve springs issue from it, repeating the specific pattern of impact causing a hidden content to break outward.
The deniers ask whether becoming dust can be followed by a new creation, treating bodily dissolution into earth as the obstacle answered by grave extraction.
The question whether bones and disintegrated fragments can be raised specifies the altered physical contents that the opened grave must surrender.
The answer to the fragmented-bones objection is that the One who created them first will restore them, preserving personal identity through material dispersal.
The people reject the promise that after death and becoming dust and bones they will be brought out, explicitly naming emergence of decomposed grave material.
A repeated objection asks whether people who have become dust and bones will be brought out, closely matching the section's depiction of grave contents extracted from soil.
The deniers ask whether they and their ancestors will be brought out after becoming dust, making خروج from earthen dissolution the disputed event.
The resurrection objection names death, dust, and bones before asking whether people will be raised, specifying what lies behind the section's content-like grave grammar.
The question whether death, dust, and bones can be followed by resurrection again identifies the grave's transformed physical contents.
The first and later generations are to be gathered at an appointed time, answering 56:47 by ensuring that no layer of the earth's accumulated dead remains uncollected.
